theme: The seven seals, the four horsemen
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 6:1-17. The Lamb opens the first six of the seven seals. Read it as a picture of the forces at work in history between Christ’s first coming and his return, and notice the cry of the martyrs and the response of the world to the wrath of the Lamb.
settingTheScene: This is the beginning of the unfolding of the scroll, with four horsemen modeled on Zechariah 1 and 6, and with words that recall Jesus’ own description of the age in Matthew 24: conquest, war, famine, death, persecution, and cosmic upheaval. Interpreters have read the seals in different ways: as events leading up to the end (futurist), as the general pattern of the whole age (idealist), as events of the first century (preterist), or as the course of history (historicist). Many see in them what Jesus described as “the beginning of the birth pains” (Matthew 24:8). In every view, it is the Lamb who opens each seal, which means that all of history is under his authority.
observation: “Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals” (v. 1).
“And its rider had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he came out conquering, and to conquer” (v. 2).
“It was granted to its rider to take peace from the earth, so that people should slay one another” (v. 4).
“And do not harm the oil and wine!” (v. 6).
“And its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed him” (v. 8).
“How long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (v. 10).
“Told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete” (v. 11).
“For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?” (v. 17).
interpretation:
The first four seals are four horsemen. Each is summoned by one of the living creatures: “Come!” The first, on a white horse, has a bow and a crown and “came out conquering, and to conquer.” Interpreters disagree about the rider. Some see Christ (compare 19:11, where Christ rides a white horse), or the gospel going out in conquest. Others see a counterfeit, the spirit of military conquest, because the horsemen that follow are all evils. The second, on a red horse, takes peace from the earth so that people slay one another, with a great sword: war and violence. The third, on a black horse, holds a balance. A quart of wheat for a denarius, a day’s wage, means famine prices: a worker could buy only enough for himself, with nothing for his family. But the oil and wine are not harmed, as though a limit were set on the famine. The fourth, on a pale horse, is Death, with Hades following, “given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts.” Notice the repeated “it was given”: they have authority only as far as God permits.

The fifth seal moves from the earth to the altar in heaven. John sees “the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.” They cry out, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” This is the cry of every martyr and every victim of injustice, and God hears it. It is not a request for private revenge but for God’s justice to be shown. Each is given a white robe and told “to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been.” God has a plan and a timetable, and the suffering of his people is part of it.

The sixth seal brings cosmic upheaval: a great earthquake, the sun black as sackcloth, the moon like blood, stars falling, the sky vanishing, every mountain and island moved. This is the language that the prophets used for the day of the Lord. Everyone, kings, great ones, rich, strong, slave and free, hides in caves and calls on the mountains and rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?” The Lamb, who is gentle, is also the judge. The wrath of the Lamb is the final answer to the cry of the martyrs.

The chapter ends with a question that the next chapter answers: “Who can stand?” The answer is those who are sealed by God (chapter 7). Until then, the church lives in an age of war, famine, death, and persecution, and the Lamb is on the throne.
connection: Zechariah 1:7-11 and 6:1-8 are the sources for the horsemen. Matthew 24:4-14 describes the same pattern of conquest, wars, famines, and persecution. Ezekiel 14:21 mentions four judgments. Genesis 4:10 speaks of the blood that cries out. Psalm 79:5, 13:1-2, and Habakkuk 1:2 ask “how long?” Luke 18:7-8 promises justice for those who cry to God. Isaiah 13:10, 34:4, and Joel 2:30-31 use cosmic language. Hosea 10:8 and Luke 23:30 describe calling on mountains. Malachi 3:2 asks who can stand. Romans 12:19 says vengeance belongs to the Lord.
application:
When news of wars, famines, and disasters weighs on you, remember that each seal is opened by the Lamb. He is not surprised.

Pray for persecuted Christians around the world, using the martyrs’ cry, “how long?”

Think about your readiness to stand before God. Thank Christ that the one who judges is the one who died for you.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that nothing happens in history outside his authority.
Tell him what makes you afraid about the state of the world.
Ask him to give you patience while you wait.
